A directed graph can represent dependencies between tasks. Topological sorting produces an order in which every prerequisite precedes the task that needs it. Such an ordering exists only when the graph has no directed cycle. A queue of vertices with zero incoming edges supports an efficient iterative algorithm.

A mutex protects shared state by allowing one thread to enter a critical section at a time. Lock ordering helps avoid deadlocks when several resources must be acquired together. Keeping critical sections small reduces contention. Tests should exercise concurrent access rather than relying only on sequential execution.

Firmware initializes hardware and provides low-level control routines. An update mechanism should verify integrity before installing a new image and preserve a recovery path if the installation fails. Version metadata and reproducible build records make debugging easier across different device revisions.

A database index trades additional storage and write work for faster lookup. The best index depends on the query pattern and the distribution of values. Measuring a representative workload is more useful than assuming that every extra index improves performance.

Unit tests validate small behaviors, while integration tests check interactions between components. Deterministic inputs and explicit assertions make failures reproducible. A passing test suite does not prove the absence of bugs, but it provides evidence that specified behaviors still hold after a change.

A compiler transforms a program through several representations. Parsing identifies structure, semantic analysis checks meaning, and optimization rewrites computations while preserving behavior. Backend code generation must respect the target instruction set and calling convention. Differential testing can compare optimized output with a simpler reference.
